title: The Adpocalypse
hook: Newspapers found big brands’ adverts running beside extremist videos. The advertisers left, and creators’ income fell with them.
situation: YouTube placed adverts automatically across millions of videos. Brands assumed their adverts appeared beside safe content, and creators assumed advertising would keep flowing.
exchange: In early 2017 The Times reported that adverts for major brands and the UK government were appearing next to extremist content. Hundreds of advertisers paused spending on YouTube.
brought: The advertisers
Budgets they could withdraw overnight, and a demand for brand safety.
YouTube
Tighter rules on which videos could carry adverts, applied largely by automated systems.
turning_point: More than 250 advertisers paused spending. YouTube responded by stopping adverts on far more videos, and many ordinary creators saw their income drop sharply. The creators called it the Adpocalypse.
measure: Advertisers reported as pausing spend. An analyst estimate that it could cost Google up to $750 million was widely quoted but not confirmed
evidence: The boycott and YouTube’s changes are well documented. Creators’ losses were reported individually rather than measured across the platform.
lesson: Creators carry the cost of a platform’s brand safety problems. Brands and creators both need income that doesn’t depend on one advertising system.
take: The Adpocalypse is why so many creators sell merchandise, memberships and products today. It taught a generation that advertising income can vanish because of something they never made.

how_to_measure: For brand safety, measure where adverts actually run, not just where they are targeted. For creators, track the share of income from sources other than platform advertising.

title: The App That Switched Itself Off
hook: Vine had made a generation of comedians famous. Twitter shut it down with three months’ notice.
situation: Vine’s biggest creators had asked for ways to earn money on the app. Many were making a living from brand deals instead, and had begun moving to YouTube and Instagram.
exchange: On 27 October 2016 Twitter announced it would discontinue the Vine app, as part of cost cuts and job losses. Vine had been bought by Twitter in 2012 and had never paid its creators directly.
brought: Vine’s creators
Six-second comedy that had built huge young audiences.
Twitter
A platform it could not afford to run and had not given creators a reason to stay on.
turning_point: The app closed to new uploads in January 2017. Its best creators had already moved, and TikTok later took up the short, looping format Vine had pioneered.
metric_label: When Twitter announced Vine would close
measure: A date. User figures for Vine at closure were reported inconsistently
evidence: The announcement and closure are well documented. The movement of Vine’s creators to other platforms is clear from their later careers but was not measured.
lesson: A platform that doesn’t pay its creators gives them every reason to leave. When they go, the audience follows them, not the app.
take: Vine didn’t fail because the format was wrong. TikTok proved the format was right. It failed because its creators were building careers somewhere else.

creative.heading: Creator media

announcement: Read about the shutdown · The Hollywood Reporter
how_to_measure: Track where a platform’s top creators earn most of their income. When it’s mostly elsewhere, the platform is at risk.

title: Dropped by Disney
hook: The biggest creator on YouTube made antisemitic jokes and called it satire. Disney and YouTube ended their deals within days.
situation: PewDiePie was signed to Disney’s Maker Studios and had a series on YouTube’s paid service. Edgy humour had helped build his audience, and he saw his jokes as aimed at the media, not at anyone else.
exchange: In February 2017 The Wall Street Journal reported that nine of his videos since August 2016 contained antisemitic jokes or Nazi imagery, including paying people to hold up an offensive sign.
brought: Felix Kjellberg
The largest audience of any individual on YouTube, and a defence that the jokes were taken out of context.
Disney and YouTube
Commercial deals and brand reputations they were not prepared to risk.
turning_point: Maker Studios ended its partnership, YouTube cancelled the second season of his series Scare PewDiePie and removed him from its premium advertising programme. He apologised for the jokes while criticising the reporting.
metric_label: When Disney and YouTube ended their deals with him
measure: A date. The financial loss was not disclosed
evidence: The deals that ended are well documented by Tubefilter, TechCrunch and others. His audience kept growing afterwards, which shows the gap between brand risk and audience loyalty.
lesson: Creator partnerships need agreed boundaries before the first video, not after the first controversy. Brands should know what a creator’s audience finds funny.
take: This is the case that showed brands the limits of working with personalities they don’t control. It also showed that losing brand deals doesn’t mean losing an audience.

how_to_measure: Before a creator partnership, review a sample of their recent content against your brand’s standards, and agree what happens if those standards are broken.

title: The First Case Against Influencers
hook: Two YouTubers promoted a gambling site they secretly owned. The US regulator brought its first ever case against individual influencers.
situation: Disclosure rules for endorsements existed, but regulators had pursued brands rather than the creators who posted. Many creators did not disclose paid or owned relationships.
exchange: Trevor Martin and Thomas Cassell, known as TmarTn and Syndicate, promoted CSGO Lotto, a site for gambling with video game items, to their young audiences without saying they owned it.
brought: The creators
Large gaming audiences, many of them teenagers.
The Federal Trade Commission
Endorsement rules, enforced against individuals for the first time.
turning_point: In September 2017 the FTC settled its first complaint against individual social media influencers, requiring the pair to disclose material connections clearly in future. It also sent warning letters to other influencers.
metric_label: When the FTC settled its first case against individual influencers
measure: A date. The settlement carried no fine but set obligations
evidence: The FTC’s own announcement documents the case. Its effect on disclosure across the industry is visible in later guidance and enforcement, not in a single number.
lesson: Disclosure is the creator’s responsibility as well as the brand’s. If you own it or were paid for it, say so plainly.
take: This case ended the idea that rules applied only to advertisers. Every disclosure label in a brief today has its roots here.
impact_source: Read about the final settlement · Tubefilter
how_to_measure: Audit a sample of creator posts each month for clear disclosure, and report the compliance rate alongside campaign results.

image.alt: A man works on a laptop beside a window
image.credit: Photograph used in the official September 2017 FTC settlement announcement; substituted still · Federal Trade Commission press page, photographer uncredited

title: The Orange Tile
hook: Hundreds of influencers posted the same orange square on one day. The festival they promoted didn’t exist.
situation: Fyre Festival promised a luxury music festival on a private island in the Bahamas. Its organisers had little infrastructure but a large marketing budget.
exchange: In December 2016 the organisers paid influencers and models, including some of the world’s best-known, to post a plain orange tile and promotional video. Most posts did not say they were paid.
brought: The influencers
Glamour and huge audiences, with little sight of what they were promoting.
The organisers
Money for posts, and a festival that collapsed when guests arrived in April 2017.
turning_point: Guests found tents and emergency supplies instead of villas. The founder was later jailed for fraud, and Kendall Jenner, reported to have been paid $250,000 for one post, settled with the bankruptcy trustee.
metric_label: Reported fee for a single influencer post
measure: A fee reported in court filings and the press, not confirmed by the influencer
evidence: The posts, the collapse and the lawsuits are well documented. The influencers’ role is clear, but their responsibility was settled in court rather than measured.
lesson: Creators lend their credibility to whatever they promote. Check what you’re selling, and disclose that you’re being paid to sell it.
take: Fyre is the cautionary tale of influencer marketing as pure reach. The orange tile worked brilliantly as an advert. It just advertised something that wasn’t real.

title: Cut from Google Preferred
hook: One of YouTube’s biggest stars filmed something he should never have published. YouTube cut him from its premium advertising programme.
situation: Logan Paul’s daily vlogs drew millions of young viewers, and he was part of Google Preferred, the programme that sold advertisers the platform’s most popular channels.
exchange: On 31 December 2017 he posted a vlog filmed in a forest in Japan that showed a person who had died. It was viewed millions of times before he took it down.
brought: Logan Paul
A huge young audience and a vlog that crossed a line most viewers recognised at once.
YouTube
Rules on what can be shown, and commercial programmes it could withdraw.
turning_point: On 10 January 2018 YouTube removed his channels from Google Preferred and put his original projects on hold. It later tightened the rules for its premium advertising programme across the board.
metric_label: When YouTube removed him from Google Preferred
measure: A date. The financial cost was not disclosed
evidence: YouTube’s actions are well documented by CNBC, Tubefilter and others. His audience and later career recovered, which shows how platform penalties and audience behaviour can diverge.
lesson: Premium advertising programmes need human review, not just audience size. Being popular is not the same as being safe for a brand.
take: This case changed how platforms sell creators to advertisers. After it, being in a premium tier meant being reviewed, not just being big.

title: The Free Stay
hook: A British YouTuber asked a Dublin hotel for a free stay in return for exposure. The owner published her email and banned every blogger.
situation: Hotels and restaurants received a growing stream of requests from influencers offering coverage in return for free stays and meals, with little agreement on what that exposure was worth.
exchange: Elle Darby emailed the White Moose Café and Charleville Lodge asking for five free nights in exchange for videos and posts. The owner, Paul Stenson, posted her email publicly with her name removed and a scathing reply.
brought: Elle Darby
A YouTube audience and a common style of collaboration request.
Paul Stenson
A combative social media style and a following that loved a fight.
turning_point: Darby was identified and posted a tearful video. The owner banned all bloggers and sent her a mock invoice. The row went round the world and became shorthand for the question of what influence is worth.
measure: A date. Both sides gained followers, which was itself part of the debate
evidence: The exchange is well documented by Tubefilter, HuffPost and others. It changed no rules but shaped how venues and creators talked about value.
lesson: Value exchanges need evidence. A creator pitch should say who the audience is and what they do, not just how many there are.
take: This row is the industry’s awkward adolescence in one email. The fix it pointed to, clear rate cards and audience data, is now standard practice.
credit: Elle Darby and the White Moose Café, 2018
impact_source: Read about the ban · HuffPost UK
how_to_measure: For hospitality partnerships, agree in advance on tracked bookings or enquiries from the creator’s audience, and compare them with the cost of the stay.

image.alt: Elle Darby wears a white top beside a clothing rack
image.credit: Contemporary creator still published with hotel-row reporting; original response not authenticated · Elle Darby, via Tubefilter

title: TanaCon
hook: A YouTuber held her own convention across the road from VidCon. It was shut down on its first day.
situation: VidCon, in Edition 01, had become the creator industry’s main event. Some creators felt it treated them badly and wanted their own events built around their fans.
exchange: Tana Mongeau announced TanaCon, a free convention with paid VIP tickets, held at a hotel near VidCon in Anaheim in June 2018 and organised with a small event company.
brought: Tana Mongeau
A big young audience and a promise of an event that put fans first.
The organisers
A venue far too small for the crowd that turned up.
turning_point: Thousands of fans queued for hours in the heat, the venue could not cope, and the event was shut down on its first day. Mongeau apologised and promised refunds.
measure: Attendance figures were disputed. The shutdown is the documented outcome
evidence: Contemporary reporting by Tubefilter, BuzzFeed News and Newsweek documents the event and its failure. The number of tickets and attendees was disputed.
lesson: An audience is not an operations team. When creators move into live events, they need partners who can deliver at the scale their audience brings.
take: TanaCon is VidCon’s cautionary twin. Both were creator-led. One had the patience to start small, the other started with the size of its audience.

title: Pledged to Disclose
hook: Britain’s competition regulator made sixteen famous names promise to label paid posts. Influence had become regulated advertising.
situation: British advertising rules required paid posts to be labelled, but many celebrities and influencers were vague, using tags that viewers didn’t notice or understand.
exchange: The Competition and Markets Authority investigated and secured formal commitments from sixteen celebrities and influencers, including Ellie Goulding and Rita Ora, to disclose clearly when they had been paid or given products.
brought: The sixteen
Recognisable names whose commitments set an example.
The CMA
Consumer protection law, and the power to take court action if commitments were broken.
turning_point: In January 2019 the commitments were published alongside new guidance. Clear labels like Ad became the expected standard in the UK, and the regulator later acted against platforms too.
metric_label: Celebrities and influencers who signed commitments
measure: The number who signed, published by the CMA
evidence: The CMA’s announcement documents the commitments. The effect on disclosure across all posts has been studied in later reports, but is not in a single figure.
lesson: Clear disclosure protects the creator, the brand and the audience. Put the label at the start, in plain words.
take: This is the British moment influencer marketing grew up. It turned disclosure from good manners into law that individuals could be held to.
how_to_measure: Track the share of a creator programme’s posts with a clear label in the first line, and test whether audiences notice it.

image.credit: Official GOV.UK announcement-page graphic, substituted still; no original commitments film authenticated · Crown copyright / GOV.UK

title: Made for Kids
hook: YouTube paid a record fine over children’s data. The creators who made children’s videos lost much of their advertising income.
situation: YouTube said it was not for under-13s, but channels for children drew huge audiences and personalised adverts ran on their videos, using data from young viewers.
exchange: The Federal Trade Commission and New York’s attorney general alleged that YouTube had collected children’s data without parental consent. Google and YouTube agreed to pay $170 million.
brought: Children’s creators
Some of the most watched content on the platform.
The regulators
Children’s privacy law, and a ruling that creators could be liable too.
turning_point: From January 2020 creators had to label videos made for children, which turned off personalised adverts, comments and some features. Many children’s creators reported steep falls in income.
metric_label: Settlement paid by Google and YouTube, a record under children’s privacy law
measure: The settlement amount, published by the FTC
evidence: The settlement is documented by the FTC. The effect on creators was reported widely but not measured across the platform.
lesson: Who the audience is matters as much as how big it is. Brands working with family creators should know the rules on children’s data and advertising.
take: This case moved the rules for children’s content from the platform to every creator. It is a reminder that audiences come with obligations.

title: The Creator Who Stepped Away
hook: One of YouTube’s most loved creators apologised for old videos and walked away from a channel of more than 20 million subscribers.
situation: In 2020 many creators faced scrutiny over offensive material in their older videos. Jenna Mourey, known as Jenna Marbles, had been on YouTube for a decade and was widely admired.
exchange: In June 2020 she posted a video apologising for past content, including a sketch in which she impersonated Nicki Minaj and another with offensive jokes, and said she was leaving her channel.
brought: Jenna Marbles
Ten years of comedy and a reputation for kindness to her community.
Her audience
Loyal viewers, many of whom asked her to stay.
turning_point: She made private many old videos and stopped posting. The channel stayed silent, and her decision became a reference point in conversations about accountability among creators.
metric_label: Subscribers on the channel she left
measure: Subscribers at the time, as reported. The income she walked away from was not disclosed
evidence: Her departure was widely reported. The case shows a creator choosing to stop rather than a platform or brand ending the relationship.
lesson: A creator’s archive is part of the partnership. Brands and creators both benefit from reviewing old content before it becomes a story.
take: This is the rare failure case where the creator set the terms. It is also a reminder that ten years of public work carries ten years of different standards.
impact_source: Read about her departure · Global News
how_to_measure: Review a creator’s back catalogue as part of due diligence, and record which older videos remain live during the partnership.

title: The Pink Sauce
hook: A private chef went viral with a bright pink sauce and started selling it. The labels and the shipping went wrong in public.
situation: TikTok made it possible for anyone to build demand for a product in days. Making food safely at scale, with correct labels and reliable shipping, still took time and expertise.
exchange: Veronica Shaw, known as Chef Pii, posted videos of a vivid pink condiment and sold bottles online. Buyers reported leaking packages, inconsistent colour and nutrition labels that did not add up.
brought: Chef Pii
A product the internet couldn’t stop talking about, and the courage to sell it herself.
Dave’s Gourmet
An established sauce maker that later partnered with her to produce it properly.
turning_point: The criticism became its own TikTok trend in July 2022. Within weeks she partnered with Dave’s Gourmet, which reformulated and produced the sauce, and it went on sale in Walmart.
metric_label: From viral launch to retail partnership
measure: A timeline. Sales figures were not published
evidence: The problems and the partnership are documented by Tubefilter, Rolling Stone and Food Network. Sales were not disclosed.
lesson: Demand is not the same as readiness. Creators launching products need manufacturing partners before the audience arrives.
take: Pink Sauce went from failure to retail in a summer. The recovery is the lesson: the creator brought the audience, and the partner brought the competence.

creative.label: Read how the chef survived her downfall · Rolling Stone
creative.heading: Creator media

impact_source: Read about the Walmart launch · Food Network
how_to_measure: For a creator product, track complaints and refunds per thousand orders in the first month, and fix supply before scaling the audience.

title: The Mascara Review
hook: A beauty creator reviewed a sponsored mascara. Viewers were convinced she was wearing false lashes.
situation: Mikayla Nogueira had built a large audience on honest, affordable beauty reviews. Sponsored reviews were common, and audiences relied on creators to show real results.
exchange: In January 2023 she posted a sponsored video for L’Oréal’s Telescopic Lift mascara. Viewers and other creators argued the result looked like false lashes, which she did not confirm or address directly.
brought: Mikayla Nogueira
Millions of followers who trusted her reviews.
L’Oréal
A paid partnership for a product the review had to show honestly.
turning_point: The video became a wider argument about trust in sponsored beauty content, nicknamed lashgate. The mascara still sold well, and the debate raised questions about advertising rules for before-and-after demonstrations.
metric_label: When the review and the backlash happened
measure: A date. No regulator ruled on the video
evidence: The controversy is documented by Glossy and others. The product’s sales were reported anecdotally. Whether false lashes were used was never confirmed by the creator or brand.
lesson: In a product demonstration, show only the product. A brief should say so, and a creator should insist on it.
take: This case shows how fast an audience will test a creator’s honesty. The trust she had built was the reason it mattered so much.

title: The Honey Investigation
hook: Creators had promoted a coupon extension for years. A YouTuber showed it was taking their commissions.
situation: Honey, a browser extension owned by PayPal, had been sponsored by many of the biggest YouTubers, from MrBeast to Linus Tech Tips. Creators also earned through affiliate links.
exchange: In December 2024 the YouTuber MegaLag published an investigation alleging that Honey replaced creators’ affiliate tags with its own at checkout, taking commissions that creators believed were theirs.
brought: MegaLag
Months of research and a clear demonstration of how the extension worked.
The creators
Years of sponsorships that had put Honey in front of millions.
turning_point: Millions of users uninstalled the extension within weeks, creators who had promoted it withdrew support, and lawsuits followed, including one led by the YouTuber LegalEagle.
metric_label: Chrome users who uninstalled Honey in the weeks after, as reported
measure: Change in the Chrome Web Store user count, as reported. Later reports put the fall higher
evidence: The investigation and the user losses were reported by Fortune, Tubefilter and others. PayPal said it followed industry rules on attribution. The lawsuits were ongoing when reported.
lesson: Creators should understand how sponsors make money from their audience. Due diligence runs both ways.
take: This is the creator economy investigating itself, and it worked. A single well-researched video did what years of sponsorship scrutiny hadn’t.

title: Fourteen Hours of Silence
hook: On a Saturday night TikTok stopped working for every American user. Creators found out what a platform risk really feels like.
situation: A US law required TikTok to be sold by its Chinese owner or banned from 19 January 2025. Creators had built businesses on it, and many had not built elsewhere.
exchange: Late on 18 January 2025 TikTok went offline in the United States, showing users a message about the law. Creators posted goodbyes and urged followers to find them on other platforms.
brought: TikTok’s American creators
Audiences they could only reach through one app.
The US government
A law that put the platform’s future in political hands.
turning_point: Service returned within about fourteen hours after President Trump said he would delay enforcement. The shutdown made creators diversify, and the platform’s future in the US stayed uncertain for months.
metric_label: How long TikTok was offline in the US
measure: The length of the shutdown, as reported
evidence: The shutdown and restoration were widely reported. How many creators moved audiences elsewhere is not measured.
lesson: Own a direct line to your audience. An email list or a second platform is insurance a creator can’t buy after the switch goes off.
take: India’s ban in Edition 04 showed what happens when a platform disappears. America got fourteen hours of the same lesson, and most of the industry took it seriously.
